title: VAE-HDC: Efficient and Secure Hyper-dimensional Encoder Leveraging Variation Analog Entropy
problem: Hyperdimensional computing requires high-dimensional vectors that consume significant memory and power resources, and current implementations expose basis vectors and parameters vulnerable to unauthorized access or security attacks.
motivation: HDC provides advantages for learning from sparse data with noise robustness and parallelism, but practical deployment requires addressing power efficiency and security concerns in hardware implementations.
method: The approach builds tiny analog circuits (10 transistors each) that exploit natural manufacturing variations in transistors to create a physically-unclonable entropy source — a way to generate high-dimensional computing vectors that can't be copied or reverse-engineered. Custom low-power circuits perform all necessary operations (entropy storage, distribution, binding, permutation, and bundling) entirely in analog form rather than converting to digital, which saves power while keeping sensitive basis vectors protected from data leakage.
key_novelty: Using natural transistor manufacturing variations as an uncopyable analog entropy source that securely encodes hyperdimensional computing vectors without ever storing them in digital form.
contributions: Novel VAE cell design with 10 transistors achieving 30.23-57.76 dB SNR entropy robustness with minimal area footprint
14.3× reduction in vector dimensions compared to binary/multi-bit HDC while improving accuracy by 2%
End-to-end analog circuit implementation enabling 48.5nJ per query with 327× leakage power reduction versus SRAM
Hardware-secured basis vectors providing enhanced security with 11 dB lower PSNR against unauthorized data retrieval

metrics.area: 1.3-4.4× reduction vs SRAM; 4.4× unit entropy cell area reduction
metrics.energy_or_tops_w: 327× leakage power reduction vs SRAM; 48.5nJ per query
metrics.other: 14.3× vector dimension reduction; 11 dB PSNR reduction (security metric)

limitations: Paper does not discuss applicability beyond HDC, scalability to other ML algorithms, or performance on general-purpose machine learning workloads.
